story.card_text:
Kennedy picked a site for his library himself, next to Harvard. After his death Cambridge residents fought it, worried about traffic and tourists, and in 1975 the library corporation gave up. UMass Boston donated land here at Columbia Point instead. The library's own page says it sits on a landfill and the site was raised 15 feet; Pei later recalled, per Wikipedia citing a WGBH interview, finding old refrigerators under the soil and methane you could light with a match.

Jacqueline Kennedy chose I.M. Pei in 1964, when, the library says, he was relatively unknown. It was dedicated on October 20, 1979, with Jimmy Carter there. The pavilion is 80 feet by 80 by 115 feet high, nearly empty, an enormous flag hanging in it. Pei wrote that visitors would be 'alone with their thoughts.'

It's ticketed, under-18s free; check before you go. Next door, the state's Commonwealth Museum is free on weekdays and keeps the 1629 charter and Adams's 1780 constitution.

story.card_text:
The Kennedys lived here from 1914 to 1920, and John was born upstairs on May 29, 1917. They outgrew it and moved out in 1920. After he was killed in 1963, the National Park Service says, the house became a focus of public mourning. In 1966 the family bought it back, and Rose Kennedy, 'relying on her memory' and a Jordan Marsh decorator named Robert Luddington, set out to make it look the way it did in 1917.

So what you tour is a mother's memory, furnished. The Park Service says many pieces are original and the rest are family pieces, antiques or reproductions. Boston Magazine put the originals at about a fifth, including the bed by the window she chose so the doctor would have light. The clocks are set to just before 3 p.m., the hour he was born. She also recorded her own voice for the tour; it still plays. 'We were very happy here.'

In 2001 the Globe reported, from a longtime associate, that Whitey Bulger once threw a Molotov cocktail through a window here; Wikipedia dates it to 1975, during the busing fight.

Tours are free, in season only, roughly late May to late October; the rest of the year, by appointment. Check before you go.

John was born upstairs in nineteen seventeen. After he was killed, people came here to mourn. In nineteen sixty-six the family bought the house back, and his mother, Rose, set out to make it look the way it did the year he was born. She worked from her own memory, with a decorator from Jordan Marsh. Some of the furniture is original. A lot of it is what she remembered, or something like it. The clocks inside are stopped just before three in the afternoon, when he was born. And she recorded her own voice for the tour. It still plays in the rooms. We were very happy here, she says. Tours are free.

story.card_text:
An antique dealer named Scott Wilson spotted a painting by the trash on a Roslindale sidewalk and took it for the frame. His friends wanted the painting. That was Lucy in the Field with Flowers, a scowling old woman floating over a meadow, and it became the first piece of the Museum of Bad Art. Its caption says 1993; BU Today dates the rescue 1994.

The museum's mission, per BU Today, is 'to bring the worst of art to the widest audience.' It spent years in a theater basement in Dedham, then in the Somerville Theatre's basement, 'conveniently located just outside the men's room.' After the pandemic it landed here in 2022, in the Dorchester Brewing taproom, in what Messy Nessy calls a Victorian former sheet-metal plant.

How big is the collection? BU Today said about 600 pieces in 2016; Messy Nessy said over 900 in 2025. Only a few dozen hang at once. Admission is free, it's open into the night, and on Friday and Saturday it's 21 and over after 6. Check before you go.

Of every room on this walk, it's the one still open after dark.

His friends wanted the painting. It's called Lucy in the Field with Flowers, an old woman frowning over a meadow, and it started the Museum of Bad Art. Its mission is to bring the worst of art to the widest audience. For years it hung in theater basements. In Somerville it was right outside the men's room. Since twenty twenty-two it's been here, over the bar of a brewery. There are hundreds of pieces in the collection, and a few dozen on the walls at a time. It stays open late. On Friday and Saturday nights it's over twenty-one after six.

seo.landing_copy:
This is a walk past Boston's oddest rooms. It's worth it from the sidewalk, better if you go in, and several of them are free. It runs from the north slope of Beacon Hill through the Common and Back Bay to the Fens, about two and three quarter hours, and every stop has an answer you can find on the street, at noon or at 9 p.m.

You'll stand outside a synagogue whose pews came from a Black church, and a Black meeting house that became a synagogue. You'll hear how Harvard students walked the State House's wooden codfish out in a flower box. You'll find a library with half a street number, a little stone building on the Common that a parks commissioner modeled on Versailles, and then the house he froze in 1936. Under a church on Newbury Street is a basement that lends out twelve-foot dragons. Then the genealogists the state evicted, a painting the legislature voted to seize, what its preservationists call the only Louis Comfort Tiffany house still standing, and a glass globe stuck in 1935.

Where it matters, each stop says whether going in is free or ticketed. Hours change, so check before you go. Three optional detours are a T ride away: the Kennedy Library on a former dump, the house where Rose Kennedy re-created her son's birthplace from memory, and a museum of bad art in a brewery that's open late.

Every fact is sourced and listed on our sources page. When a famous story is shaky, we tell the story and then what the records say.

Any two stops are free. Walk them and decide.

story.card_text:
The wooden pews in this synagogue came from a Black church. Jewish immigrants from the province around Vilna, now Vilnius in Lithuania, organized on Beacon Hill in 1888, and their first real home was the old Twelfth Baptist Church at 45 Phillips Street, a Black congregation's meetinghouse. When the city took that building by eminent domain around 1916 to expand a school and paid them $20,000, they built this one, cornerstone 1919, designed by Max Kalman, whom the West End Museum calls the only Jewish architect in Boston. And they carried the pews over. The West End Museum says those pews had seated people who escaped slavery and men who volunteered for the 54th Massachusetts.

Inside, the megillah holders next to the ark are pickle barrels wrapped in red velvet, per the Forward. The walls carry three layers of Eastern European folk murals, each one painted over before the next. Restorers didn't know they were there until 1998. The last member, Mendel Miller, held the final service in 1985.

Sources disagree on when they bought the Baptist church: 1902 or 1906. Inside opens for tours and events, per the Vilna Shul; check before you go.

The city took it to expand a school, paid them twenty thousand dollars, and they built this place, starting in nineteen nineteen. Here's the part to remember. They took the pews with them. The West End Museum says those benches had held people who escaped slavery and soldiers who joined the fifty-fourth Massachusetts. Inside, the stands for the scroll of Esther are pickle barrels covered in red velvet. The walls hold three layers of folk murals, each one painted over before the next, and nobody knew they were there until nineteen ninety-eight. The last member locked up after the final service in nineteen eighty-five.

story.card_text:
From 1904 to 1972, this Black meeting house was a synagogue. The Baptist congregation that built it sold it in 1898 and moved to the South End, and by 1904 it was Congregation Anshi Libavitz. It stayed a synagogue until 1972, when the Museum of African American History bought it. So on this short stretch of the north slope, a Black church became a synagogue, and a synagogue was furnished from a Black church. Same neighborhood, two directions.

The tablet by the door names the man who got it built. The National Park Service says Cato Gardner, a native of Africa, personally raised $1,500 toward it, and African American craftsmen did most of the work. It was finished in 1806 for a Baptist congregation that had formed the year before with 24 members, 15 of them women.

It was a school, a lecture hall and a political room as much as a church. William Lloyd Garrison founded the New England Anti-Slavery Society here in 1832. In 1863 it was a recruiting post for the 54th Massachusetts. Going inside takes a reserved ticket from the museum; check before you go.

The Park Service says Gardner, who was born in Africa, raised fifteen hundred dollars of the cost himself, and Black craftsmen did most of the building. It was finished in eighteen oh six. William Lloyd Garrison started the New England Anti-Slavery Society in this room in eighteen thirty-two. During the Civil War, men signed up here for the fifty-fourth Massachusetts. And then, in eighteen ninety-eight, the congregation sold it and moved to the South End. By nineteen oh four, this was a synagogue. It stayed one until nineteen seventy-two. So, a few doors apart: a Black church that became a synagogue, and a synagogue sitting in pews from a Black church.

story.card_text:
In the vaults of this library is a book whose cover says it is bound in a highwayman's skin. It's the 1837 Narrative of the Life of James Allen, who died in the state prison that July. The story goes that he asked for a copy bound in his own skin and given to John Fenno, the man who fought him off in a robbery. The cover label reads, in Latin, This book is bound in the skin of Walton, one of his aliases. Is it? Wikipedia says the Anthropodermic Book Project confirmed it. Rare Book Monthly says human and goat are hard to tell apart and the provenance is foggy. Call it contested. It's viewable by appointment, not on display.

The rest of the place is nearly as odd. It grew out of the Anthology Society in 1807 and is still a membership library. The Athenaeum says its Proprietors' Shares hit 1,049 by 1858, after paying for this building, and the number hasn't moved since. Shares get handed down in families like silver; today one is a $5,000 contribution plus dues. Non-members can pay to see the first floor only; check before you go.

The building opened in 1849, designed by Edward Clarke Cabot. You'll see his work again in four stops.

story.card_text:
Before he made a lady for New York Harbor, Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi modeled this frieze in Paris, and Italian workmen carved it in place, up on the 170-foot tower. Four scenes, one per side: baptism, communion, marriage, death. Per Bartholdi's own letter, quoted in the Boston Journal in 1902, the faces include Charles Sumner, Longfellow, Emerson, Hawthorne, Lincoln and Garibaldi, and his mother sits beside Lincoln.

H. H. Richardson designed the church for the Brattle Square Unitarians; it was dedicated in December 1873 and the frieze finished in late 1874. The four angels at the corners blow long horns pointed down, which got it the nickname Church of the Holy Bean Blowers. The congregation that built it couldn't pay for it and dissolved; it went up for auction in 1881 and was deeded to the First Baptist Church in 1882.

The trumpets were restored and the scaffolding came down in the summer of 2025, after nearly ten years up; the city put $1,245,000 in Community Preservation money into the building's repairs. It's a working church, so the outside is the stop, and the gilded horns are easiest to count in daylight.

Bartholdi wrote that he put real faces in it. Longfellow. Emerson. Hawthorne. Lincoln. Garibaldi. And his own mother, sitting next to Lincoln. story.card_text:
In June 1922 the Massachusetts legislature passed a bill to take a painting out of this library. It hangs upstairs, at the top of the main stairs, in the Sargent Gallery: John Singer Sargent installed it in phases until 1919, the Triumph of Religion, about 600 pieces of raised relief and, here and there, metal and glass jewels.

One panel, Synagogue, shows Judaism as a blindfolded, cowering figure, the medieval way. The library says it drew criticism at once, inside and outside the Jewish community. Per Globe and New York papers of the time, as cited in the painting's Wikipedia entry, Representative Coleman Silbert's bill to seize it by eminent domain passed the House on June 6 and the Senate on June 9. It was repealed in 1924 as unconstitutional. Someone smeared ink on it; per the library, Sargent repaired it himself. It's still up, with signs explaining it.

Same building, second free room: the Leventhal Map Center, about 200,000 maps and 5,000 atlases, gallery free with no ticket. story.card_text:
The world in here still has Siam and the Soviet Union in it. You cross a glass bridge about 30 feet long through the middle of a hollow globe made of 608 stained-glass panels, the earth turned inside out so that, from the center, every point on it is the same distance from your eye. It opened June 1, 1935, designed by Chester Lindsay Churchill, the architect of this building, with glass by the Rambusch Company of New York.

The borders are frozen. Which year exactly is a small fight: Wikipedia says the panels follow Rand McNally maps from 1934; the Inquirer says 1935 maps; the church says it shows the world as it was in 1935. Either way, it predates World War Two. The church says Churchill meant it to be updated as borders changed. It never was. Wikipedia's account, citing the Times and the Globe, says updates were weighed in 1939, 1958 and 1966 and dropped, partly over cost, partly because the old map had become the point.

Glass doesn't absorb sound. Whisper at one end of the bridge and someone at the other end hears it at their ear. It's a timed ticket, kids free; check before you go.

It opened in June of nineteen thirty-five, and the borders have never been changed. So you'll see Siam instead of Thailand, and the Soviet Union. The architect meant for it to be updated. It never was. Now the trick. Glass doesn't soak up sound. Whisper at one end of the bridge, and someone at the other end hears you like you're standing next to them. story.card_text:
The Massachusetts Historical Society owns tea from the Boston Tea Party. Some of it floated across to Dorchester Neck, and on the morning of December 17, 1773, someone gathered tea leaves on that shore. They ended up in a small glass bottle, and the Society still has it. Its chief historian and librarian, Peter Drummey, told NBC Boston the tea floated across the harbor and someone scooped some up and kept it. Who, nobody has said.

The Society was founded in 1791 by Jeremy Belknap and nine others. It calls itself the oldest organization in the country devoted to collecting the materials of American history. This building, by Edmund M. Wheelwright, went up in 1899. Its galleries are free; the Society says so on its own page. Check hours before you go.

Call it the oldest takeout in Boston. The bottle isn't always out, so ask at the desk. On your way in, look down at the two middle columns: one base says MHS, the other 1154.
